docs.title: Install and start tC4
docs.summary: Download the build for your computer, install or unpack it, and start the app. It opens on the Home screen.
docs.where: Your computer's Downloads folder, then the tC4 app or the start-tc4.sh launcher
docs.text: translationCore 4 (tC4) is a desktop app for Bible translation. It runs on Windows, macOS (Apple silicon) and Linux. Everything it needs to start drafting in English-gateway projects comes in the download: the source texts, the translation helps, and the Open Bible Stories pictures. You do not need the internet to start. The first time you use tC4 on a computer, and each time a new pre-release comes out. Get the build for your computer from the tC4 releases page: the .exe installer for Windows, the .pkg installer for macOS, or the .zip for Linux. Windows: run the .exe. Windows SmartScreen warns about an unsigned app: choose More info , then Run anyway . Start tC4 from the Start menu or the desktop shortcut. macOS: open the .pkg. If macOS blocks it, open System Settings › Privacy & Security and choose Open Anyway . The installer asks for an administrator password. Then start translationCore 4 from Applications. Linux: unpack the zip, open a terminal in the unpacked translationCore4 folder and run ./start-tc4.sh. Wait for the window. tC4 opens on Home, with the heading Your projects. To start your first project, click + Add a project. See The Home screen. Builds made before 27 September 2026, including v4.0.0-alpha.7, open on an older Home screen with the heading "Your Bibles". See What changed in The Home screen. Only one copy of tC4 runs at a time. Starting it again brings you back to the window that is already open. On Linux the launcher may print a note that it starts "with --no-sandbox". That is expected for an unpacked zip. Your projects are kept in a pankosmia/tc4-projects folder in your home folder. See Where your projects are kept. Windows: on a computer that never had the Microsoft Visual C++ runtime, tC4 says "The backend could not be started". Install the Visual C++ Redistributable (x64) from Microsoft first (issue 284). The installers are not signed yet, so your computer warns you the first time (issue 44). On macOS, quitting may leave the bundled server running (issue 206). The window keeps the system frame (issue 214). Linux has no installer and no menu entry. Start it from a terminal. This is pre-release software. Do not use it for production translation work yet. The window opens on Home within about 30 seconds, with the heading Your projects. With no projects yet, Home says "No projects yet. Select + Add a project to start." No error banner shows.

docs.title: The Home screen
docs.summary: Home lists your projects, most recently used first. From here you open a book or story, add a project with + Add a project, share a project to Door43, and open its Settings.
docs.where: Home — the first screen. Click the tC4 logo, or the project name in the top bar, to come back to it.
docs.text: Home is where you start. At the top is the heading Your projects. The top bar on Home has only the tC4 logo on the left and the round Door43 account icon on the right. Below the heading, Home shows: The Resume banner : the project, book and chapter (or story) you last edited, and what you last edited, for example Sample Titus · Titus 1 and Last edited verse 3 — "y a su tiempo". Click it or Resume → to go back. See Resume where you left off. + Add a project on the right, above the list. The project list , with the project you used most recently at the top. The Door43 account is the person icon at the upper right, on Home and inside a project. When nobody is signed in, its name is Door43 account: not signed in. See Share to Door43. A project card Each project is one card: The name , for example Sample Titus, with a LTR or RTL badge for the text direction. An Open Bible Stories project also has an OBS badge. A project you just imported has an Imported badge. A line under the name with the language code, the number of books, how many are in progress, and where the project lives. For example: "es · 1 book · 1 in progress · Only on this computer". A stories card says "es · 50 stories · 1 in progress · 1% drafted · Only on this computer". The line shows the language code (es), not the language name (Español). The name is in Settings. Share on Door43 and Settings on the right. Settings opens the Project settings dialog. See Project settings. Book tiles (one per book, with its draft percentage) and an Add a book tile. A stories card shows the stories you edited most recently, and Show all {n} stories → to see all fifty. When you have no projects yet, the list is empty and says "No projects yet. Select + Add a project to start." The Add a project dialog + Add a project opens a dialog called Add a project: "Start a new translation or bring in one you have already started." It has three cards: Card What it says What it opens --- --- --- New Bible "Translate books of the Bible, verse by verse." Create a Bible project New Open Bible Stories "Translate the 50 Open Bible Stories, frame by frame." Start an Open Bible Stories project Import a project "From translationCore 3, USFM files or a Scripture Burrito." Import a project Every time you start tC4, and whenever you want to change to another project or book, or add a new project. Start tC4. Home opens. To open a book, click its tile on the project card. A new book (or a new project, or an import) that has no remembered place opens in Understand. A book you have worked in opens where you left it, in the same mode. To start a new project or bring one in, click + Add a project. In the Add a project dialog, click the card you want: New Bible, New Open Bible Stories or Import a project. To close the dialog without choosing, press Esc, click the round ✕ at the top right, or click outside the dialog. To change a project's settings, click Settings on its card. To come back to Home later, click the tC4 logo or the project name at the top left. The list moves. The project you opened last jumps to the top. If you click quickly after coming back to Home, make sure the card under the pointer is the one you want. Keyboard: after you open + Add a project, press Tab to move through the three cards (a blue ring shows which one is selected), then press Enter or Space to open it. Esc closes the dialog. The dialog always opens on the three cards, even if you closed it part way through an import. A card with more than 12 books shows only the books in progress. Click Show all {n} books → to see every book, and Show in-progress books only → to shrink it again. A book tile that shows a dash (—) instead of a percentage means the app has not read that book's progress yet. It is not 0%. If a project fails to open, Home shows "The project could not be opened." with the reason. If the project list itself could not be read, a Retry button appears. What changed in Increment 8: the Project settings button left the top bar; open settings from the card's Settings button instead (issue 505). The top bar no longer shows a server name such as "QA server", and a card says "Only on this computer" or "Shared at owner/repo" without a server name (issue 506). Known issue: The message "{name} was imported · {books}" does not close by itself. It stays at the bottom of Home, and can cover a card's buttons, until you close it with its ✕ or another message replaces it. Known issue: Only the newest import keeps the Imported badge. When you import another project, the badge moves to the new card. Known issue: Right after you start tC4, a project card can say "0 in progress" and its book tiles a dash (—), then show the real percentage a little later without you opening anything. Known issue: After you join verses into a span, the book's percentage can go down (for example from 7% to 4%) even though no text was lost. Home shows draft progress only. Checking progress is shown inside Check (issue 139). Home shows the language code on each card, not the language name. The heading Your projects is at the top, with PROJECTS and the blue + Add a project button on the right. The top bar on Home has only the tC4 logo and the round Door43 account icon. There is no server name (such as "QA server") and no Project settings button. When nobody is signed in, the icon's name is Door43 account: not signed in. Each project card shows its name, a LTR or RTL badge, and a line such as es · 1 book · 1 in progress · Only on this computer. Each card has Share on Door43 and Settings. The cards are in most-recently-used order. The project you opened last is at the top. + Add a project opens the Add a project dialog with three cards, in this order: New Bible, New Open Bible Stories and Import a project. With no projects yet, Home says "No projects yet. Select + Add a project to start." Each Bible project card has one tile per book with a draft percentage bar; the last tile is Add a book. Each Open Bible Stories card has an OBS badge and story tiles.

docs.title: Understand, Translate and Check — the three modes
docs.summary: Every open project has three modes. Understand the passage, Translate it, then Check it — in any order.
docs.where: Top bar, centre — the Understand · Translate · Check switch (shown while a project is open)
docs.text: When a project is open, the top bar shows a three-way switch: Understand — read the source passage with its translation notes, word links and questions, and write your own comments. See Read a passage before you translate. Translate — draft your translation beside the source texts. See The Translate screen. Check — check your draft with Translation Notes and Translation Words, align words, and preview the book in Community Checking. See Choose a checking tool. Open Bible Stories projects have the same three modes. A book or story you open for the first time starts in Understand, so you read before you draft. After that, tC4 opens it in the mode you used last. The top bar also shows the project name (click it to go back to Home), the save indicator (Saved or Unsaved changes) and the Door43 account icon. Project settings are not in the top bar; they open from the project's card on Home. Any time. The order is up to you: many teams read in Understand first, draft in Translate, then check. Open a project book (or story) from Home. Click Understand, Translate or Check in the top bar. The screen changes; your place in the book stays the same. Changing mode saves a checkpoint of your work if anything changed (see Saving and checkpoints). tC4 remembers the last mode you used. The Resume banner on Home takes you back to it, and so does the book tile. What changed in Increment 8: a new book used to open in Translate. It now opens in Understand (issue 507). The "Internet" or "Local" status left the top bar; the account icon replaced it. When you click Check, tC4 goes back to the checking tool you used last, not the list of tools. To pick another tool, click ← All checking tools at the top left. Publishing is not a separate mode. Export lives inside Check › Community Checking. See Export a book as PDF. The switch shows three choices; the selected one is filled. Changing mode keeps the same book and chapter (or the same story). A new book, a new story project, or an imported book with no remembered place opens in Understand. The top bar shows no Project settings button and no server name in any mode. At the right there are only the save indicator and the account icon.

docs.title: Saving and checkpoints
docs.summary: tC4 saves as you work. The indicator at the top right tells you the truth about your last save, and offers Retry if a save failed.
docs.where: Top bar, right side — the save indicator
docs.text: You never need a Save button for the project. Each edit — a verse, a check decision, an alignment, a comment — is saved when you finish it. The indicator in the top bar shows one of: Indicator Meaning --- --- Saved Everything you did is saved. Saving… A save is running. Unsaved changes You have typed something that is not saved yet (for example, an editor is still open). Save failed — retry A save did not work. Your text is kept; press Retry. Checkpoint not saved The project checkpoint did not finish. Your work is saved; press Retry. A checkpoint is a saved version of the whole project. tC4 makes one when you change mode or leave the project, and only if something changed. Glance at it before you close the app. If it says Saved, all your work is saved. Make an edit, for example draft a verse and click outside the editor. Watch the indicator: Saving…, then Saved. If it shows Save failed — retry or Checkpoint not saved, click Retry. On the desktop app, closing the window waits for a save that is being retried. If a checkpoint fails when you leave a project, Home shows a warning. Open the project again and tC4 tries again. There is no history view of your own changes yet (issue 78). After you finish an edit, the indicator shows Saving… and then Saved. If a save fails, it shows Save failed — retry with a Retry button.

docs.title: Resume where you left off
docs.summary: The Resume banner on Home takes you straight back to the book, chapter and mode where you last made a change — Understand, Translate, or the checking tool you were using — even after you close and restart the app.
docs.where: Home — the dark blue Resume banner at the top, with the Resume → button
docs.text: Home shows a dark blue banner at the top with the project name, the book and chapter (or the story), and what you last changed. For example: Sample Titus · Titus 1 — Last edited verse 3 — "y a su tiempo" (after drafting verses) Sample Titus · Titus 1 — Last edited verse 1 (after a checking decision on verse 1) Sample Stories · Story 1 — Last edited frame 2 — "Al principio..." (after drafting a story) Click the banner, or its Resume → button, to go straight back. tC4 opens the same place in the mode you last used : Understand, Translate, or Check with the same checking tool (for example Translation Words). Each time you come back to tC4. Work in a project: draft a verse, write a comment, or decide a check item. Go back to Home (click the project name at the top left), or close tC4 and start it again. Click the banner, or its Resume → button. tC4 opens the same book and chapter, in Understand, Translate or Check — whichever you used last. In Check it reopens the same tool. The banner follows your last change , not the last book you opened. If you open a book only to read it, the banner still shows the place you last changed. The project you opened last moves to the top of the list on Home. Each book tile also remembers where you were in that book, and its mode. Each story tile remembers the frame you last worked on. A checking decision counts as a change. After you mark an item in Check, the banner names that verse, and Resume returns to the checking tool. Known issue: After you join verses into a span and save the section, the banner can still name a verse that no longer exists on its own (for example "verse 3" after verses 2 and 3 became 2-3). Resume still opens the right chapter. Known issue: Resume into a story opens the story at the top, not at the frame named in the banner. Scroll down to the frame. Known issue: For a stories project, the frame number in the banner can change after you only decide check items (for example from frame 2 to frame 0, then frame 1), and the quote can disappear. The quote in the banner can stop in the middle of a word. Resume is per computer. It does not follow you to another computer. The banner names the project and the book and chapter (or story), and the last edit, for example Sample Titus · Titus 1 and Last edited verse 3 — "y a su tiempo". Clicking it opens the same book and chapter (or story) in the mode you last used — Understand, Translate or Check — and in Check, the same checking tool. The banner follows your last change (a drafted verse or frame, a comment, or a checking decision). Only opening a book does not change it.

docs.title: Switch project or go back Home
docs.summary: Click the project name at the top left to leave the project and return to Home, where you can open another project or book.
docs.where: Top bar, left — the project chip (initials and name). Its tooltip says Switch project.
docs.text: The top bar shows the project you have open: its initials, name and language code. Clicking it (or the tC4 logo) takes you back to Home. To open another project, add a book, or open project settings. With a project open, point at the project name at the top left. The tooltip says Switch project. Click it. Home opens. Click a book or story tile in any project to open it. To move to another book of the same project, you do not need Home: use the book list on the left of Translate or Understand. See Open a book and move between chapters. None known. Home opens and lists all projects. If you changed anything, a checkpoint is saved as you leave.

docs.title: Create a Bible project
docs.summary: A Bible project is one translation in one language and one text direction. Name it, give the language, choose the direction, and add books next.
docs.where: Home › + Add a project › New Bible
docs.text: The New Bible dialog creates a new, empty Bible translation project on your computer. The subtitle says it well: "You'll add books next. Everything here can be changed later." The fields are: Bible name — for example "Kanuri Bible". The first letters and digits of the name also name the project folder. Language name and Code — the language you translate into, for example "Kanuri" and knc (the code for Central Kanuri). Text direction — Left to right or Right to left. Checking language — the gateway language your team checks and aligns against. English ships with the app and has the complete set of book packages, so it is preselected and has a RECOMMENDED badge. Under it: "unfoldingWord · ULT + UST, notes, words — installed with the app". The English texts and helps that come with this build are the v91 releases, so a new project needs no download to start. Script font — the font your translation is shown in. It starts on "Noto Sans (default)". The other choices are Charis SIL, Scheherazade New (Arabic script), Awami Nastaliq (Nastaliq) and Padauk (Myanmar). Versification (folded away) — the verse numbering scheme. Opened, the list is rso, vul, rsc, lxx, eng (default), and org. eng (default) is selected. Under the list: "Most projects keep the default." No other scheme was chosen. When you start translating into a new language, or want a separate practice project. On Home, click + Add a project. In the Add a project dialog, click the first card, New Bible. The New Bible dialog opens in its place. Type a Bible name, for example Help Demo Titus. Type the Language name and the language Code, for example Kanuri and knc. Under Text direction, click Left to right or Right to left. Leave Checking language on English (it is already selected). Optional: choose a Script font, or open Versification to pick another numbering scheme. Click Create Bible →. The Add a book dialog opens straight away. Continue with Add a book. The first book you add opens in Understand. The name must contain at least one Latin letter or digit, because it names the project folder. If a project folder with that name already exists, tC4 tells you ("A project folder named … already exists") — choose another name. Keyboard: in the Add a project dialog, press Tab until the New Bible card has a blue ring, then press Enter or Space. Esc closes the dialog. If you close the dialog without creating (with Cancel or the round × at the top right), nothing is saved. The New Bible dialog has no back button. To choose another kind of project, click Cancel, then + Add a project again. It opens on the three cards. On a small screen the dialog may not fit. Scroll inside it to reach the top fields or the Create Bible → button. Known issue: Some language codes are refused, even ones that look right. On an earlier build, kau (Kanuri as a whole) was refused with "Language code 'kau' is not custom (no 'x-') but has not been found in the BCP47 lookup table", even though the Code field shows "e.g. kau" as its example (screenshot 4). On this build, typing kau and leaving the field did not show that warning. Use the code for your specific language instead, such as knc for Central Kanuri. Known issue: If you start typing the moment you click into a field, the first letters can be lost. Wait a moment before you type, and check the name before you create the project. You can change the text direction and script font later in Project settings. The project name, language name and code cannot be changed after creation yet ("Renaming arrives with a later increment."). Only English is offered as the checking language when you create a project. You can change it later in Project settings if another language's notes are installed. See Change the checking language. Whole books only. "Passage sets come later." The New Bible dialog shows Bible name, Language name, Code, Text direction, Checking language (English, Recommended) and Script font. After Create Bible → the Add a book dialog opens straight away. The new project appears on Home.

docs.title: Add a book
docs.summary: Add one book, or several at once, to a Bible project. The drafting sources (unfoldingWord ULT + UST v91) come with the app, and a new book opens in Understand.
docs.where: Home › a Bible project card › Add a book tile (also opens by itself after Create Bible →)
docs.text: The Add a book dialog adds whole books to a Bible project. The first step is Start a blank book: "Pick a book of the Bible and draft from verse 1. The unfoldingWord source package downloads automatically." The book step names the drafting sources: "Drafting sources: unfoldingWord ULT + UST v91 — installed with the app." These English sources come with tC4, so you can start without an internet connection. Right after you create a Bible project, and any time you want to start another book. On Home, click the Add a book tile on your project card. (After Create Bible → this dialog opens by itself.) Click Start a blank book. Choose the book in the Book list, for example Titus (TIT) . To add several books at once, click Choose several at once → and click each book in the New Testament and Old Testament grids. Click Pick one book → to go back to the list. Click Create book (or Create {n} books). The new book opens in Understand at chapter 1, so you can read the passage and its helps first. Click Translate when you are ready to draft. After that, opening the book from Home returns to the mode you used last. Use a short book such as Titus, Philemon or 3 John for practice. ← Back returns to the first step without adding anything. The first step still says the source package "downloads automatically", while the book step says ULT + UST v91 is installed with the app. On this build the new book used the v91 texts that came with the app: the source pane in Translate says "unfoldingWord Literal Text · v91 · pinned". A book that is already in the project cannot be picked again (it shows ✓, "Already in this Bible"). Removing or replacing a book is not available. Book introductions cannot be drafted yet (issue 55). To bring in a book you already translated elsewhere, use Import a project. It always creates a new project; importing into an existing project is planned (issue 365). The book step opened on Genesis (GEN), with "Genesis · 50 chapters · Old Testament". In a project that already has Titus, the open list shows Titus (TIT) with a check. In Choose several at once, Titus is greyed and checked, and the other books are buttons. The sources line reads: Drafting sources: unfoldingWord ULT + UST v91 — installed with the app. After Create book the new book opens in Understand at chapter 1, not in Translate.

docs.title: Open a book and move between chapters
docs.summary: Click a book tile on Home to open it. Inside the project, the book list on the left moves you between books and chapters.
docs.where: Home › a book tile; inside the project, the Books · {n} list on the left (toggle it with Toggle book list)
docs.text: A project can hold many books. On Home each book is a tile. Inside the project, the left-hand list ( Books ) shows every book of the project with its draft percentage. The open book is highlighted and shows a grid of its chapter numbers. When a project opens, tC4 reads its saved work first. For a large project you see Opening the project… with steps such as "Reading the journal" and a count of saved actions. Whenever you want to work on a different book or chapter. On Home, click a book tile, for example Titus . A new book with no remembered place opened in Understand. If you last worked in Translate, it opens there again. In Translate or Understand, look at the list on the left. If it is hidden, click the Toggle book list button at the top left of the page. Click a chapter number to go to that chapter. Click another book's name to open that book. The book and chapter title above the text (for example "Titus 1") tells you where you are. Each book remembers where you were, so a tile takes you back to the same place. None known. While a project opens, a small window says Opening the project… with a progress bar. The book list shows each book with its draft percentage; the open book shows its chapter numbers. Clicking a chapter number shows that chapter; clicking another book opens it.

docs.title: Import a project (translationCore 3, USFM or Scripture Burrito)
docs.summary: Bring existing work into tC4 as a new project — from translationCore 3 project zips, USFM files, or a Scripture Burrito zip. Nothing is created until you confirm.
docs.where: Home › + Add a project › Import a project
docs.text: The import screen turns files from other tools into a new project on this computer. It accepts three kinds of file: Kind Files What comes across --- --- --- translationCore 3 project (tC3) .zip exported from translationCore 3, one or many (one language at a time) The text, and the alignments and checking decisions tC3 recorded USFM files .usfm, .sfm or .txt, one or many, one file per book The text only Scripture Burrito one .zip containing metadata.json and ingredients/ The text. A burrito exported by tC4 also brings its alignments and checking decisions. Bible and Open Bible Stories burritos both work. "Each import creates a new Bible. Nothing on this computer is changed until you confirm." To move a translation from translationCore 3 (tC3) into tC4. To start from a USFM draft made in another program. To restore or move a project exported from tC4 as a Scripture Burrito (see Export a project as a Scripture Burrito). On Home, click + Add a project. In the Add a project dialog, click the third card, Import a project. The import opens at "Import · step 1 of 3". Choose the kind of file: translationCore 3 project, USFM files or Scripture Burrito. Drop your files on the drop area, or click it to choose them in the "Open Files" window. The file appears under "1 file". Remove a wrong file with its ✕ button. Click Review files →. Read Review what was found (step 3 of 3). On the left, What was found lists each book with its chapters, verses and drafted verses, and the counts of books and files. On the right, Checks shows three rows: License, Details and Missing verses. A green dot means all is well; an orange dot means you need to look. Check the Bible name and Language code under Read from the file. Change them if they are wrong. If Details is orange and says "The language code is missing or not valid. Enter it below.", the Language code box is outlined in red with "Enter a language code such as kau or es-419." Type the code (for example es). Details turns green and Import as a new Bible becomes active. If the Bible name is already used on this computer, the box is outlined in red with "A project with this name is already on this computer. Change the Bible name, then import again." Type another name; the message goes away. A tC4 Scripture Burrito shows Carried over from translationCore 4 with the number of aligned verses and checking decisions it brings. A translationCore 3 project shows Carried over from translationCore 3 . For a translationCore 3 import, the Resource versions check is orange: "Look up on Door43 the resource versions this project used (translationNotes, the original-language text), or use the versions on this computer." Choose Look up on Door43 (this needs the internet; click Continue if "Use the internet?" appears) or Use installed versions. Import as a new Bible stays off until you choose. After the look-up the check turns green and names what it found, for example "The versions this project used were found: unfoldingWord/en tn v87, unfoldingWord/el-x-koine ugnt v0.34." Click Import as a new Bible. tC4 shows Creating your Bible… (for a small book this may flash by too fast to see). Home opens with the message "{name} was imported · {books}", for example "Tito was imported · Titus". The new card is at the top of the list and carries the Imported badge. Click a book tile on the new card. A book with no remembered place opens in Understand at chapter 1. Use ← Choose another kind or ← Choose other files to go back a step. On step 1, ← Back takes you back to the three cards of Add a project. Keyboard: in the Add a project dialog, press Tab until the Import a project card has a blue ring, then press Enter or Space. Esc closes the dialog. If you close the import part way (Esc, the ✕ button, or a click outside the dialog), nothing is created, and + Add a project opens on the three cards the next time. USFM never carries a language. A USFM file has no language code, so tC4 always leaves the Language code empty for USFM. Type it yourself. The Bible name comes from the file's \h line (for example "Tito"). USFM: each file must start with an \id line so tC4 knows the book. Two files for the same book are refused. A regional code such as es-419 is kept. The review explains: "The Bible is stored under "es"; the full tag es-419 is kept in its details." The new card shows es-419. A Scripture Burrito can hold several books. "Equipo Ejemplo — Tito y Jonás" showed BOOKS 2 (Jonah and Titus) and the new card had both tiles. An imported USFM project has no source texts pinned yet. Its Understand screen says "This project pins no source texts, so there is no source passage to show." Add sources from Project settings › Manage source texts →. translationCore 3: all the zips must be in the same language. The review counts what comes across from translationCore 3: verses, alignments, checking decisions and contributors. translationCore 3: the versions Look up on Door43 finds may not be on this computer. The new project's helps panel then says "The pinned resource is not on this computer yet. Get it from Source texts." Download them from Project settings › Manage source texts →. Importing the same translationCore 3 zip a second time gives the same Bible name, so the name-in-use message appears. Type another name, for example cfm fbt 2. Damaged files are refused. If a file cannot be read, the review shows a red "This file cannot be imported" box with the reason and a code (for example import.damaged.usfm-parse), and Import as a new Bible stays greyed. Nothing is created. See Messages that protect your project. Known issue: The message "{name} was imported · {books}" does not go away by itself, even in later imports. It can cover the bottom of the import dialog (the ← Choose other files and Cancel row) and the cards on Home. Close it with its ✕. Known issue: Only the newest import keeps the Imported badge. Import another project and the badge moves to the new card. Known issue: After you type the language code yourself, Details still says "Language and name were read from the file", although you typed the code. Known issue: For a damaged file, the Checks column can still show green Details and "Every verse is present." under the red box. The red box is the one that counts: nothing can be imported. Known issue: The carried-over count says "1 verses" for one verse. Opening a translationCore 3 project's book straight after the import used to turn the window white in an older build. In build 79d3017 it opened every time (three imports in a row). If a screen still cannot be drawn, tC4 shows "This screen could not be shown." with Back to Home , and Window › Reload (Ctrl+R) brings the app back without quitting. See If the app closed unexpectedly. Import always makes a new project. Importing a book into an existing project is planned for 4.1.0 (issue 365). A project folder name is made from the Bible name using only plain letters and digits, so "Jonás" becomes jon s in the folder name. The card shows the full name. When no license is found, the review says "No license was found in the files. None is applied." (issue 392). The dialog title is Import a project and moves through "Import · step 1 of 3", "step 2 of 3" and "step 3 of 3". Step 1 has ← Back at the bottom. The review lists each book with its chapters, verses and drafted verses, and three checks: License, Details and Missing verses. A USFM file never carries a language code: Details is orange ("The language code is missing or not valid. Enter it below.") and Import as a new Bible stays disabled until you type a code. Then Details turns green. If the Bible name is already on this computer: "A project with this name is already on this computer. Change the Bible name, then import again." Import stays disabled until you change the name. A tC4 Scripture Burrito shows Carried over from translationCore 4 with its alignments and checking decisions. A translationCore 3 project shows Carried over from translationCore 3 and an orange Resource versions check with Look up on Door43 and Use installed versions. Import as a new Bible stays off until you choose one. After the Door43 look-up it reads "The versions this project used were found: …". A damaged file shows "This file cannot be imported" with the reason and a code such as import.damaged.usfm-parse or import.damaged.truncated. Nothing is created. After Import as a new Bible Home shows "{name} was imported · {books}", the new card carries an Imported badge, and its book opens in Understand.

docs.title: Export a book as PDF
docs.summary: Make a print-ready, dated PDF of the open book, laid out with your Page setup choices.
docs.where: Check › Community Checking card › Open → › Export › Export PDF
docs.text: The PDF export typesets the open book the way the Community Checking preview shows it: the book title, each drafted chapter, your choice of columns, spacing, paper size, drop caps and verse numbers. The file name carries the book code and today's date. To print a draft for reviewers or community checkers, or to share a readable copy. Open the book and click Check in the top bar. If the last checking tool you used opens instead of the list, click ← All checking tools. On the Community Checking card, click Open →. Optional: set the Page setup (see Community Checking preview and page setup). Click Export, then Export PDF. A save window opens with a suggested file name. Keep it or type another, then save. When the file is saved, the panel shows "Saved <file name ", for example "Saved TIT-2026-10-05.pdf". Close the message with its ✕. Chapters with no drafted verse at the start or end of the book are left out. A run of undrafted chapters in between prints as one line, such as "[ chapters 5–7 not yet drafted ]". Undrafted verses print as "[ verse not yet drafted ]". If nothing is drafted in the book, tC4 refuses and names the book, for example: "Philemon has no drafted verse yet, so the PDF has nothing to print. Draft at least one verse of this book, then export the PDF again." No save window opens and no file is made. The PDF follows the Page setup: with Letter the page is US Letter, with A4 it is A4. Set the page setup each time you open the screen; it is not remembered. If you cancel the save window, no message shows and no file is made. If the download is interrupted, tC4 says "… did not finish downloading. Export it again." On Linux, the save window is the system file window. Its title bar shows a long "blob:http://127.0.0.1…" address; that is normal. It opens in your Downloads folder, with the suggested name selected in the Name field. On this build its Save and Cancel buttons were above the visible part of the window: press Enter to save, or Esc to cancel. Exporting does not change your project. At most it saves one checkpoint of work you had not checkpointed yet. The PDF export needs the desktop app. It is not offered when tC4 runs in a web browser. Footnotes are not printed yet (the Footnotes switch is disabled). End-to-end testing of right-to-left and complex scripts in the PDF is planned after 4.0 (issue 29). The Export menu lists Export PDF, USFM, aligned, USFM, plain and Scripture Burrito (.zip). A save window offers a file named like TIT-2026-10-05.pdf (book code and today's date). Only after the file is saved, the panel shows "Saved TIT-2026-10-05.pdf". If you cancel the save window, no message appears. For a book with nothing drafted, tC4 refuses: "{Book} has no drafted verse yet, so the PDF has nothing to print. Draft at least one verse of this book, then export the PDF again." No save window opens.

docs.title: Export a book as USFM (aligned or plain)
docs.summary: Save the open book as a USFM file — with your word alignments woven in, or plain text only.
docs.where: Check › Community Checking › Export › USFM, aligned or USFM, plain
docs.text: USFM is the standard text format for Bible translations. tC4 can export the open book two ways: USFM, aligned — your text with the word alignments to the original language included, the format other alignment-aware tools read. USFM, plain — just your text, without alignment data. The file is written outside the project. Your project does not change (apart from a checkpoint). To hand a book to another program, a typesetter, or a reviewer who works in USFM. Open the book and click Check. If the last checking tool you used opens instead of the list, click ← All checking tools. Click Open → on the Community Checking card. Click Export. Click USFM, aligned or USFM, plain. A save window opens with a suggested file name. Keep it or type another, then save. When the file is saved, the panel shows "Saved <file name ", for example "Saved TIT-aligned-2026-10-05.usfm". If you cancel, no message appears. Align your verses first if you want the aligned file to carry alignments. See Link and unlink words. Until you align, USFM, aligned and USFM, plain give the same text: there are no alignments to weave in yet. Unlike the PDF, USFM export does not refuse a book with nothing drafted. A verse span you joined is written as one verse, for example \v 2-3. On Linux, the save window is the system file window. Its title bar shows a long "blob:http://127.0.0.1…" address; that is normal. It opens in your Downloads folder, with the suggested name selected in the Name field. On this build its Save and Cancel buttons were above the visible part of the window: press Enter to save, or Esc to cancel. On Windows the plain USFM export does not download in this build (issue 425). Known issue: The book's header lines (\h, \toc1–\toc3, \mt) contain the book code (for example TIT), not the book's name. Edit them in the file if another program needs the name. Known issue: Undrafted verses are written with a placeholder. USFM, aligned saves a file named like TIT-aligned-2026-10-05.usfm. USFM, plain saves a file named like TIT-2026-10-05.usfm. The panel shows "Saved <file name ".

docs.title: Export a project as a Scripture Burrito
docs.summary: Save the whole project — text, alignments and checking decisions — as one Scripture Burrito zip. Works for Bible and Open Bible Stories projects.
docs.where: Check › Community Checking › Export › Scripture Burrito (.zip)
docs.text: A Scripture Burrito is the open, standard package format tC4 uses for every project. Exporting one gives you a single zip of the whole project: every book (or all fifty stories), your alignments and your checking decisions. tC4 can import it again as a new project. To keep a copy of the project somewhere safe. To move the project to another computer and import it there (see Import a project). To give the project to another Scripture Burrito tool. Open the project and click Check. If the last checking tool you used opens instead of the list, click ← All checking tools. Click Open → on the Community Checking card. Click Export, then Scripture Burrito (.zip). A save window opens with a suggested file name. Keep it or type another, then save. When the file is saved, the panel shows "Saved <file name ", for example "Saved Sample Titus-2026-10-05.zip". If you cancel, no message appears. Stories also offer this zip. Their Export menu lists Export PDF, Story Markdown (.zip), and Scripture Burrito (.zip). See Export stories as PDF or Markdown. The zip holds every book of the project, not only the open book. To bring the zip back into tC4, on this or another computer, use + Add a project › Import a project › Scripture Burrito. The review shows what carries over from tC4 (alignments and checking decisions). See Import a project. On Linux, the save window is the system file window. Its title bar shows a long "blob:http://127.0.0.1…" address; that is normal. It opens in your Downloads folder, with the suggested name selected in the Name field. On this build its Save and Cancel buttons were above the visible part of the window: press Enter to save, or Esc to cancel. To put a project on Door43, use Share on Door43 on its Home card instead (see Share to Door43). A file named after the project and today's date, like Sample Titus-2026-10-05.zip, is saved. The panel shows "Saved <file name ".

docs.title: The Translate screen
docs.summary: Translate shows the source text on the left and your translation on the right, one row per section, with the book list and the helps panel beside them.
docs.where: Top bar › Translate
docs.text: Translate is where you draft. The screen has four parts: The book list (left) — books and chapter numbers. Hide or show it with Toggle book list. The source column — the text you translate from. Tabs switch between the literal text (ULT), the simplified text (UST) and the original language (Greek for the New Testament, Hebrew for the Old). Under the tabs is the source's full name and pinned version, for example "unfoldingWord Literal Text · v91 · pinned". Your translation — one row per section, beside the matching source text. At the top right is the Section / Verse switch that chooses how you draft. The helps panel (right) — notes, word links, questions, the simplified text and your comments for the verses you are working on. Hide or show it with Toggle helps panel. Whenever you draft or revise your translation. Open a book from Home (or click Translate in the top bar). Choose a chapter in the book list on the left. Read the source text in the left column. Switch tabs to compare ULT, UST and the original language. Choose Section to draft a whole section at once, or Verse to draft one verse at a time. Start drafting: see Draft a section or Draft or revise one verse. On Sample English, Titus 1 is one section, verses 1–3. Verse 1 is already drafted ("Paul, a servant of God.") and it shows in the section row, with the numbers 2 and 3 after it. The section is not finished, so Draft section 1–3 is still there. Sections follow the source text's section breaks, so your rows line up with the source. tC4 remembers your Section / Verse choice for each project. ULT and UST cannot be shown side by side yet; use the tabs or the helps panel's simplified tab (issue 353). The helps panel cannot be widened yet (issue 234). If a project uses verse numbering that differs from the source, Translate works verse by verse only ("Verse view. This project's verse numbering differs from the source, so sections are not available."). The page title reads the book and chapter, for example "Titus 1". The left column has source tabs (ULT, UST, Greek or Hebrew) and the source text; the right column is headed with your project name and language code. Each row is one section of the chapter; an undrafted section shows a Draft section {span} button.

docs.title: Source tabs — gateway texts and the original language
docs.summary: Switch the source column between the literal text, the simplified text and the Greek or Hebrew original.
docs.where: Translate › source column tabs. This Spanish project shows GLT · GST · Greek. An English gateway shows ULT · UST · Greek (or Hebrew in the Old Testament).
docs.text: The source column can show three texts for the same passage. On this Spanish project the tabs are: GLT — the literal gateway text. GST — the simplified gateway text. Greek — unfoldingWord Greek New Testament. An Old Testament book uses Hebrew instead. An English gateway names the first two tabs ULT and UST. The Greek and Hebrew texts come with the app. The gateway texts are the ones pinned for the project. Compare the literal and simplified texts to understand the meaning, and look at the original when a word is unclear. In Translate, look at the tabs above the source column. Click GLT, GST, or Greek. On an English project, click ULT, UST, or Greek / Hebrew. The source text changes; your translation column stays the same. When you point at a note or word link in the helps panel, the matching words in the source are highlighted. The same tabs appear in Understand. The section span follows the text in the source tab. On Sample English, ULT and UST both show Titus 1:1–3 and Draft section 1–3. Greek shows Titus 1:1–16 and Draft section 1–16. The drafted verse stays: "Paul, a servant of God." Captions: "unfoldingWord Simplified Text · v91 · pinned" and "unfoldingWord Greek New Testament · v0.34 · pinned". The verse 1 note quotes the text of whichever tab is selected. UST verse 1 shows curly braces around "write this letter to you, Titus. I". Those braces are part of the source, not words to type. The source was switched back to ULT. If the text is missing for a book, the column says "This source is not available for this book." or "This source text is not on this computer." See Browse and download source texts. The selected tab is filled; the caption names the text and its pinned version, such as "unfoldingWord Greek New Testament · v0.34 · pinned". Greek shows left to right; Hebrew shows right to left.

docs.title: Draft a section
docs.summary: Type a whole section as one piece of text, then place the verse numbers. This is the main way to draft in tC4.
docs.where: Translate › Section › Draft section {span} on a section row
docs.text: Section drafting lets you translate the way you think — a paragraph or a thought at a time — instead of verse by verse. You type the section's text straight through in Type mode, then switch to Place verse numbers to put each verse number where that verse begins. For first drafts. Most translators draft whole sections. In Translate, make sure the switch at the top right says Section. On the row you want, click Draft section {span} (for example "Draft section 1–3" for the first section of Titus 1). The editor opens in Type mode. Type your translation of the whole section. Click Place verse numbers and place each number (see Place verse numbers). Click Save section. To change a saved section later, click its Draft section {span} label on the row again. Clicking the saved text itself does not open the editor. You can also type the verse numbers yourself in Type mode: start a line with the number, for example 2 Then he said…. tC4 reads it as the start of verse 2. The first verse number of a section is fixed at the start. When you reopen a saved section, Type mode shows each verse number as a plain number at the start of its line. If you press Enter between a number and its first word, the number looks as if it stands alone on a line. It is still saved at the start of that verse. Cancel closes the editor without saving the section. Press Enter for a new paragraph and Tab for a poetry line. See Paragraphs and poetry. While an editor is open, the Section / Verse switch is disabled. Known issue: If you start typing the moment the editor opens, the first letters can be lost. Wait a moment after it opens, and check the start of your text before you save. A verse number you leave in the To place bank is saved as an empty verse (not drafted). Renumbering verses in the editor is planned for 4.1.0 (issue 364). The editor card opens under the section, headed "Drafting 1–3" with a Type Place verse numbers switch. After Save section the verses show in your translation column with their numbers, and the save indicator shows Saved.

docs.title: Place verse numbers
docs.summary: After typing a section, pick up each verse number and click the word where that verse begins.
docs.where: Translate › section editor › Place verse numbers
docs.text: In Place verse numbers mode the section's words are shown one by one and each verse number is a small marker. Numbers not placed yet wait in the To place bank. You move a number by picking it up and clicking the word its verse begins with. After you type a section in Type mode, or when a verse boundary is in the wrong place. In the section editor, click Place verse numbers. Click a number in the To place bank to pick it up. Point at words: a ghost marker shows where the number would land, and the tooltip explains, for example "Begin verse 2 at Paul". Click the word where that verse begins. Repeat for every number, then click Save section. To move a number already placed, pick it up from the text and click another word. A number cannot pass another number ("Verse N cannot pass another verse number"). The first number of the section is fixed ("Verse N begins the section and is fixed"). Dropping a number onto a word where another verse already begins joins the two into a verse span. See Make or break a verse span. Switch back to Type at any time to fix words; the numbers you placed are kept. Known issue: When you pick up a number that was already placed, the bank can still say "Every verse is placed…" next to "Click the word where verse N begins". Follow the "Click the word…" hint. See the known issue under Tips. Every word shows separately; unplaced numbers wait in the To place bank. The hint reads "Pick a number up, then click the word it begins at." and, while a number is held, "Click the word where verse N begins". When all numbers are placed: "Every verse is placed. Pick a number up to move where its verse begins."

docs.title: Make or break a verse span
docs.summary: Join two or more verses into one span, such as 2–3, when your language needs to reorder their content. Break the span again the same way. Bible projects only.
docs.where: Translate › section editor › Place verse numbers (or a line starting 2-3 in Type)
docs.text: A verse span (also called a verse bridge) is two or more verses translated as one unit and numbered, for example, 2-3. Many languages need spans to put information in a natural order. In tC4 you make a span by putting two verse numbers on the same word, and break it by moving one of them away. Note: Verse spans exist only in Bible projects. Open Bible Stories are drafted by frames and have no verse numbers. When the natural way to say two verses in your language mixes their content, so the verse boundary cannot be kept. Open the section in the editor with its Draft section {span} label and type the text. Click Place verse numbers. Pick up the later verse number (for example 3). Click the word where the earlier verse (2) begins. The tooltip says "Join verse 3 to verse 2 at …". Click Save section. The verses are saved as one span, numbered 2-3. To break the span: open the section again with its Draft section {span} label, click Place verse numbers, pick up the 3 and click the word where verse 3 should begin. Click Save section. In Type mode you can also start a line with the span, for example 2-3 …. The source pane shows bridged verses too, in both directions. When you make or break a span, tC4 marks the checks and alignments of those verses as needing review. Nothing is deleted. See Editing a verse you already checked or aligned. Not available in Open Bible Stories projects. How check decisions on member verses should be handled after a span change is still an open question (issue 219); for now they are marked invalid and kept. While you hold a number over a word where another verse begins, the tooltip reads "Join verse 3 to verse 2 at <word ". After Save section the verse number shows as a span, for example "2-3". Checks and alignments on the joined verses are marked invalid and kept, so you can re-check them.

docs.title: Draft or revise one verse
docs.summary: Switch to Verse to draft a single verse, or to fix one verse without opening the whole section.
docs.where: Translate › switch to Verse › Draft verse {n} pill, or click a drafted verse
docs.text: In Verse view each verse is edited on its own. It is handy for small corrections and for translators who prefer verse-by-verse work. To correct a word in one verse. To draft one verse at a time. In Translate, click Verse in the switch at the top right of your translation column. For an empty verse, click its dashed Draft verse {n} pill. For a drafted verse, click its text (tooltip: Edit this verse). Type in the editor ("Type your translation of this verse…"). Click Save verse, or simply click outside the editor. To throw away your change, click Cancel instead. While the editor is open, the verse's place in the paragraph shows Editing below. The helps panel follows the verse you are editing. A verse span cannot be made in Verse view; use Place verse numbers. Undrafted verses show a dashed Draft verse {n} pill; drafted verses show their text. The editor is headed "Drafting N" and has Save verse and Cancel. Clicking outside the editor also saves; the save indicator shows Saved.

docs.title: Paragraphs and poetry
docs.summary: Start a new paragraph with Enter and indent a poetry line with Tab while you type a section.
docs.where: Translate › section editor › Type — press Enter or Tab
docs.text: In the section editor's Type mode: Enter starts a new paragraph. Tab indents the current line as poetry. Press Tab again for a second level, Shift+Tab to take an indent back. When your translation needs paragraph breaks, or when you translate poetry such as Psalms or quoted hymns. Open a section in the editor (Draft section {span}). Type the text. Press Enter where a new paragraph begins. At the start of a poetry line, press Tab. Place the verse numbers and click Save section. The source text's paragraphs and poetry indents show in the source column too, so you can follow them. Other formatting (headings, footnotes, character styles) cannot be added in the editor yet. The hint in the editor reads "Enter for paragraph, Tab for poetry. Place the verse numbers next." After saving, the paragraph break and the poetry indent show in your translation column.

docs.title: The helps panel in Translate
docs.summary: While you draft, the helps panel shows the notes, word links, questions, simplified text and your own comments for the verses in focus.
docs.where: Translate › right side panel — tabs Notes · Words · Questions · GST · Comments (an English gateway shows UST instead of GST)
docs.text: The helps panel puts the translation helps next to your draft: Notes — translation notes, with links to Translation Academy articles. Words — Translation Words links for key terms, with "Read the article →". Questions — translation questions with their answers, to test your draft's meaning. GST — the simplified text of the chapter. An English gateway labels this tab UST. Comments — the user comments you wrote in Understand (only in Translate). While you draft, to check what a phrase means or how a key term is defined. In Translate, if the panel is hidden, click Toggle helps panel at the top right. Click a tab: Notes, Words, Questions, GST or Comments. Open a section or verse editor: the panel narrows to the verses you are editing. Point at a card to highlight its words in the source column; click it to keep the highlight. Long notes show Show more / Show less. On Sample English the English tabs are Notes, Words, Questions, UST and Comments. Words for Titus 1:1–3 starts with Paul, a servant, of God and an apostle. Each card says Key word and Read the article →. Questions starts with "What was Paul's purpose in his service to God?" and also shows "What was the relationship between Titus and Paul?" The UST tab heading is "Simplified text · meaning-based", and verse 1 contains curly braces. Comments says "Nothing in this chapter." The panel was put back on Notes. Each help tab is explained in the Understand section. Known issue: The Comments tab labels a comment written on a section with the section's first verse, for example "VERSE 1" for a comment on the section 1–3. The panel cannot be widened yet (issue 234). The Translation Academy tab was removed from the panel in alpha.6; open articles from a note's Translation Academy → link instead. The panel has the tabs Notes, Words, Questions, GST, and Comments. With no comment written, Comments says "Nothing in this chapter." While a section or verse editor is open, the panel shows only the helps for those verses.

docs.title: Editing a verse you already checked or aligned
docs.summary: When you change a verse that has check decisions or alignments, tC4 flags them for review. Nothing is deleted.
docs.where: Translate (the edit), then Check (the flags)
docs.text: Your checks and alignments are tied to the exact words of a verse. When you change those words, tC4 keeps every decision and alignment but marks the ones that may no longer fit, so you can look at them again. A check decision whose words changed becomes Invalid . An alignment keeps the links the edit did not touch. Only the changed words come loose and go back to the word bank, and the verse's valid mark is taken back. Nothing to switch on — it happens by itself. Visit Check after you revise checked verses. Check a verse (for example mark a Translation Notes item ✓ Mark valid) and align it. Go to Translate and change a word in that verse. Go back to Check and open the tool. Read the notice at the top. Click the Invalid filter to see the items that need review, and decide them again. Open Align for the verse, place the loose words from the word bank, and click ✓ Mark valid again. Making or breaking a verse span also marks the checks and alignments of those verses for review. A checking tool may reopen at the item you were on, not the first one that needs review. Use the Invalid filter to find them all. Align shows no "The draft changed since this alignment was made" notice in this case, and the verse shows as to do (grey), not invalid: tC4 kept the links, so only the loose words need placing. Look for words back in the word bank. The notice appears when tC4 could not keep the links. See the known issues under Tips. In a checking tool, a notice says "N decision(s) no longer match the draft text and need re-review. Nothing was discarded." The affected items appear under the Invalid filter. In Align, the changed word is back in the word bank (for example "25 of 26 words placed") and the verse shows as to do again in the rail.

docs.title: Read a passage before you translate
docs.summary: Understand shows the source passage section by section, with its helps beside it and a box for your own comments.
docs.where: Top bar › Understand
docs.text: Understand is a reading screen. It shows the gateway source text of the chapter split into sections (or single verses), and the translation helps for the part you select. Many teams read and discuss a passage here before drafting it. Before you draft a passage, and whenever the team discusses meaning. Open a book and click Understand in the top bar. Pick the chapter in the book list on the left (Toggle book list shows or hides it). Choose the source with the ULT or UST tab. A Spanish gateway uses GLT and GST instead. Choose Section or Verse next to Comment by to read by sections or by single verses. In Verse view, Titus 1:1 is its own block, and the empty comment box says "What does this verse mean, and what will be hard to render?" Click a block to select it. The helps panel on the right shows the notes, word links and questions for that block. Point at or click a help card to highlight the words it is about. A small green dot on a block's header means you have written a comment there. The helps panel has Notes, Words, Questions and the simplified text tab. See the other pages in this section. Your section/verse choice is shared with Translate. Section breaks follow the gateway text. The same chapter can be one block in one language and several blocks in another. English Titus 1 starts as Titus 1:1–3. Spanish Titus 1 starts as Titus 1:1–16. Under the ULT tab, Understand names the text "unfoldingWord Literal Text". It does not show the pinned version. Translate does. Understand shows the gateway texts (ULT, UST). The Greek or Hebrew original is shown in Translate and Check. If the project uses different verse numbering from the source, Understand shows single verses only, and some verses may be noted as having "no place in the source's verse numbering" (issues 118, 121). The title reads the book and chapter with the line "Read the passage and its helps before you translate." The source tabs sit above the passage. On this Spanish project they are GLT and GST. An English gateway shows ULT and UST. The Comment by Section / Verse switch is there too. Each section is a block with its reference, the source text and a comment box. On Sample Titus the first block is "Titus 1:1–16". On Sample English the first block is "Titus 1:1–3", because the English literal text breaks the chapter there. The helps panel on the right shows the helps for the selected block.

docs.title: Translation notes and Translation Academy articles
docs.summary: Translation notes explain hard phrases verse by verse. Each note can link to a Translation Academy article that teaches the translation issue behind it.
docs.where: Understand or Translate › helps panel › Notes › Translation Academy →
docs.text: Translation Notes (tN) are short explanations of difficult words and phrases in the source text. Many notes point to a Translation Academy (tA) article, a short lesson about a translation issue such as metaphors or implied information. When a phrase is hard to understand or hard to express in your language. In Understand, click a section (or verse) to select it. In the helps panel, click Notes. Read the note cards. Point at one to highlight its phrase in the passage. Click Translation Academy → on a note to open its article. Close the article with ✕. Notes follow the project's checking language. On Sample Titus they are Spanish (Latin American), and they work offline once that package is installed. On Sample English the notes are English. The first card is labeled vintro, "Titus 1 Chapter Introduction", and it has Show more. The next card is v1 and quotes "for the faith of the chosen people of God and knowledge of the truth". Opening Translation Academy on that note highlights the phrase and opens "Abstract Nouns". ✕ closes the article. If you see "Shown from the English fallback", the checking-language notes are not on this computer and the English notes are shown instead. If an article is missing from the installed resources, the panel says "The pinned resources do not carry the article for this check." The note itself still shows. The English chapter introduction shows a raw link in the note text: "rc://ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns". It is visible as written. It is not a button. A note card shows a label such as vintro or a verse number, the phrase it is about, and the note text. Long notes have Show more. Translation Academy → opens the article inside the panel. This one is Sustantivos abstractos, with a ✕ to close it.

docs.title: Word links (Translation Words)
docs.summary: Word links point out the key biblical terms in the passage and link each to a Translation Words article that defines it.
docs.where: Understand or Translate › helps panel › Words › Read the article →
docs.text: Translation Words (tW) are short articles about important terms such as grace , apostle or righteous . The word links (TWL) connect each occurrence of such a term in the passage to its article. To translate key terms consistently and accurately. In Understand, select a section. In the helps panel, click Words. Point at a card to see which word it is about in the passage. Click Read the article → to read the definition and translation suggestions. Close the article with ✕. The same terms become check items in Check with Translation Words. On Sample English the four cards for Titus 1:1–3 are Paul, a servant, of God and an apostle. Opening Paul highlights "Paul" in the passage and shows the article "Paul, Saul". It begins: "Paul was a leader of the early church who was sent by Jesus to take the good news to many other people groups." The cards stay in the list above the article. ✕ closes it. None known. On a Spanish project each card is marked Key word, names the term in the gateway text (Pablo, siervo, de Dios, apóstol) and shows an English gloss. On an English project the card title is the phrase in the text (Paul, a servant, of God, an apostle). Under it is the article's short name (paul, servant, god, apostle). Each card says Key word and Read the article →. Read the article → opens the Translation Words article in the panel. Pablo is highlighted in the passage.

docs.title: Translation questions
docs.summary: Translation questions ask what the passage says. Use them to test whether your translation communicates the meaning.
docs.where: Understand or Translate › helps panel › Questions
docs.text: Translation Questions (tQ) are simple comprehension questions for each passage, with answers. Ask them of someone who reads or hears your translation to see if the meaning comes through. After drafting, or during community checking. In Understand (or the helps panel in Translate), select a section. Click Questions. Read each question and its answer. If a chapter has no questions, the tab says "Nothing in this chapter." or "Nothing for the verses in focus." On Sample English, Titus 1:1–3, the first question is "What was Paul's purpose in his service to God?" The answer begins "His purpose was to establish the faith of God's chosen people". The next ones are "When did God promise everlasting life to his chosen people?", "Does God lie?" (Answer · No.), and "To whom did God entrust his proclamation at the right time?" None known. Each card shows a question and, under it, "Answer · …".

docs.title: The simplified text tab
docs.summary: The helps panel can show the meaning-based simplified text of the chapter next to what you are reading.
docs.where: Understand or Translate › helps panel › the tab named after the simplified text (GST here, UST for English)
docs.text: The simplified text says the meaning plainly. The helps panel has a tab for it, named after the text. On this Spanish project the tab is GST. An English gateway shows UST (unfoldingWord Simplified Text). When the literal text is hard to follow, or to compare meaning while you read the ULT in the main column. Open the helps panel in Understand or Translate. Click the simplified-text tab. On a Spanish project it is GST. On an English project it is UST. Read the chapter's simplified text. In Understand and Translate you can also switch the main source to the simplified text with the source tabs (GST here, UST for English). Open Bible Stories have no simplified text, so the tab is not shown there. On Sample English, the English simplified text of Titus 1 shows curly braces in the first sentence: "{write this letter to you, Titus. I}". They show in the helps panel and in the source column when UST is selected. The caption under the source tab is "unfoldingWord Simplified Text", with no version. The braces are on screen. They are not part of the translation. In a Spanish project the tab is labeled GST. It shows "Simplified text · meaning-based" and the chapter's simplified Spanish text. On Sample English the tab is labeled UST. The heading is "Simplified text · meaning-based". Titus 1 begins "I, Paul, {write this letter to you, Titus. I} am a servant of God".

docs.title: Write a user comment
docs.summary: Write down what a passage means, who is speaking, and what will be hard to translate. Your comments are saved with the project and shown in Translate.
docs.where: Understand › the comment box under each section or verse
docs.text: A user comment is your own note about the meaning of a section or verse. It is stored with the project, survives closing the app, and is shown to you while you draft. While you study a passage, to record decisions and questions before drafting. In Understand, choose Section or Verse next to Comment by. Click in the comment box under the section or verse. Type your comment. Click outside the box. The comment is saved (watch the save indicator). Later, in Translate, open the helps panel and click Comments to read it. In Section view, if you wrote separate comments on single verses inside the section, tC4 tells you and suggests switching to Verse view to see each one. Edit a comment by changing the text and clicking outside again. Known issue: In Translate's Comments tab, a comment written on a section is labelled with the section's first verse (for example "VERSE 1"). A saved comment cannot be emptied: "A saved user comment cannot be emptied — user comments are permanent in this version." Edit the text instead. Comments are separate from check comments. See Write a check comment. In Section view the box's hint reads "What is this section saying? Who is speaking, to whom, and what will be hard to render?" In Verse view the hint reads "What does this verse mean, and what will be hard to render?" On Sample English, Titus 1:1 is its own block. Nothing was typed. When you click outside the box the comment is saved; a green dot appears on the block's header. The comment appears in Translate › helps panel › Comments.

docs.title: Choose a checking tool
docs.summary: The Check screen lists the checking tools for the open book and how far you have got in each.
docs.where: Top bar › Check › Choose a checking tool
labels: No items in this book yet
docs.text: Check is where you review your draft systematically. The list of tools lets you pick one. Each tool is one focused pass through the whole book, and tC4 remembers your place in each. Each card shows your progress: a bar, a count such as "2 of 157 resolved", and the next item to check. There is no "ready" label: a card that is ready to use simply shows its progress. A label appears only when the tool cannot open yet, for example Needs downloading. After you have drafted some or all of a book. Open a book and click Check in the top bar. The first time, the list of tools opens. After that, Check takes you back to the tool you used last; click ← All checking tools at the top left to see the list. Look at the progress on each card. Click a card to open the tool. Its link says Start checking →, Continue → or Review →. Community Checking says "Open →". To come back to this list from inside a tool, click ← All checking tools. The card also names the next item, for example "Next: “grace” · 1:4". When everything is decided it says All resolved — review any item. On Sample English the four cards are Translation Words (0 of 182 resolved, Next: "Paul" · 1:1, Start checking), Translation Notes (1 of 157 resolved, Next: "of the chosen people of God" · 1:1, Continue), Align (0 of 1 verses aligned, Next: verse 1:1, Start checking) and Community Checking (Whole chapter, Next · read Titus 1 aloud, Open →). "Whole chapter" is the reading scope, not an error. Align counts drafted verses only. No tool was opened. "A tool that is not ready never blocks the rest of your work." You can keep drafting while a resource downloads. If a card says Needs downloading or Unavailable offline, click Fix this… (see Fix a missing resource). You can move between a Bible project and a stories project freely. Each project's tools use that project's own notes and words: Titus uses the Bible notes (en tn) and words (en tw), and a story uses the story notes (en obs-tn) and the story word list (en obs-twl). Earlier builds could wrongly say "This book is not in the pinned resource" after a switch; that was fixed in Increment 8 (issue 434). The Align card counts only drafted verses or spans. On Sample Titus, with 1:1 and the span 2-3 drafted, it said "0 of 2 verses aligned". With nothing drafted it says No items in this book yet. Known issue: The count and the "Next:" line on a card can lag behind what you did in the tool. For example, the card can say "1 of 157" when the tool says "2 of 157 resolved", or name an item you already marked valid. The count inside the tool is the right one. Checks exist only for verses you have drafted. An undrafted verse says "This verse is not drafted yet. Draft it first, then return to check." The heading reads Choose a checking tool with the line "One focused pass through the whole book. Your place is saved in each tool." For a Bible book four cards appear, in this order: Translation Words, Translation Notes, Align and Community Checking. For a story there are three: Translation Words, Translation Notes and Community Checking (no Align). Each checking card shows a progress bar, a count such as "0 of 182 resolved" or "1 of 157 resolved", the next item, and a link such as Start checking → or Continue →. Community Checking says "Open →". With nothing drafted, Align says "No items in this book yet". A card shows a state label only when something is wrong: Needs downloading, Unavailable offline, No resources pinned or Not available for this book.

docs.title: Check with Translation Notes
docs.summary: Work through every note in the book that links to a Translation Academy article, and confirm how your translation handles each one.
docs.where: Check › Translation Notes card
docs.text: The Translation Notes tool builds a checklist from the notes that point to a Translation Academy article, such as figures of speech, implied information or passive voice. For each one you find the words in your translation that render the quoted phrase and decide whether they are right. After drafting, to check hard translation issues one by one. Click Check, then the Translation Notes card. If the last checking tool you used opens instead of the list, click ← All checking tools. Read What to check. The quoted phrase is highlighted in the gateway pane. On the Spanish checking language that pane was GATEWAY · GLT, and the quote was "conforme a la fe". It is not always the English ULT. Click "Learn more: … →" if you want the full lesson. Under Your translation, tap the word or words that render the quote. Decide: see Decide on a check item. Marking an item does not move you on. Click the → arrow at the top right of the item (above the quote) to go to the next item. On Sample English the tool opens at Item 2 of 157, Titus 1:1, quote "of the chosen people of God". Progress is 1 of 157 resolved, and To do is 156. The first rail row, "for the faith of the chosen people…", has a green dot and is not the open row. Sort is By verse. The resource line is git.door43.org/unfoldingWord/en tn · v91 · primary gateway language. Learn more says Active or Passive. The gateway pane is Gateway · unfoldingWord Literal Text, and it highlights the quote. Your translation reads "Paul a servant of God", the same missing comma and period as in Translation Words. Nothing was marked. The notes come with the app: a new project checks against the English notes v91 (en tn), with no download. A Bible project and a stories project each use their own notes. After you check a story, Titus still opens on the Titus notes (fixed in Increment 8, issue 434). By category groups items by translation issue (all metaphors together, for example). This is useful to learn one issue at a time. If the draft changes after you decided an item, tC4 marks the decision for re-review: "{n} decision(s) no longer match the draft text and need re-review. Nothing was discarded." Only notes with a Translation Academy link become check items. Other notes stay in the helps panel. The item shows What to check with the note, the original-language and gateway texts (the quote is highlighted in the gateway text), and Your translation with the verse. The rail on the left lists items, with filters and two Sort buttons, By verse and By category. Learn more: {title} → opens the Translation Academy article in a drawer.

docs.title: Check with Translation Words
docs.summary: Check every key term in the book against its definition, so important words are translated accurately and consistently.
docs.where: Check › Translation Words card
docs.text: The Translation Words tool lists every occurrence of a key term (such as God , grace , apostle ) in the book. For each, you find how you translated it and decide if it is right. To make sure key terms are consistent across the book. Click Check, then the Translation Words card. If the last checking tool you used opens instead of the list, click ← All checking tools. In the rail, next to Sort, click By word to see all occurrences of one term together (it is selected at first), or By verse to go through the book in order. Read the term. Click its "Learn more" link for the full article. If the verse is drafted, tap the word or words in Your translation that render the term. If it is not, the pane says to draft it first and come back. Decide: ✓ Mark valid, Invalid or To do. Marking an item does not move you on. Click the → arrow at the top right of the item (above the quote) to go to the next item. By word is the fastest way to catch inconsistent renderings: go through all "grace" items one after another. On Sample English the first item is Titus 1:1, "Paul", Learn more: Paul, Saul. The resource line is git.door43.org/unfoldingWord/en tw · v91 · primary gateway language. Filters read All · 182, To do · 182, Invalid · 0. By word is selected, and the visible rail starts at Admonish while Paul is the open item. The gateway pane is labeled Gateway · unfoldingWord Literal Text, and Paul is highlighted. Greek is shown and is not highlighted. Your translation reads "Paul a servant of God". On Translate the same verse is "Paul, a servant of God." The comma and the period are not in the check pane. Nothing was tapped or marked. Known issue: The term is highlighted in the gateway pane (here labeled GLT). The Greek pane shows the verse but does not highlight the term. After you go to Translate and back to Check, tC4 reopens Translation Words where you were. Known issue: With By word, the open item and the rail can disagree. On Sample Titus the open item was Paul, but the rail started at Admonish and did not show Paul as selected. Screenshot 1 (an earlier build) shows the same thing with Pablo. None beyond the general check limits and the known issues under Tips. The item shows the term Pablo, Learn more: Pablo, Saulo, the Greek text, and the gateway text labeled GLT with Pablo highlighted. Your translation says "This verse is not drafted yet. Draft it first, then return to check." Next to Sort in the rail are two buttons: By word (all occurrences of a term together, selected at first) and By verse.
